strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile computer vision problem: editing an image to evoke a target emotion using only an image and an emotion label. Its focus on semantic changes beyond recoloring is useful.
EmoPair provides a potentially valuable resource of 338,544 image pairs. The curation pipeline identifies its underlying InstructPix2Pix and EmoSet sources and describes its filtering criteria.
Randomized human comparisons provide evidence beyond classifier scores. The reported 56% aggregate online preference suggests that the approach produces useful emotional transformations.
The qualitative examples demonstrate varied edits, and the manuscript meaningfully discusses semantic drift, facial artifacts, and potential misuse for emotional manipulation.
weaknesses: The main automated evaluation is coupled to the method: the same predictor P labels training images, filters generated training pairs, selects outputs during up to 20 inference iterations, and computes EMR/ESR. EMR drops from 50.20% to 5.06% without P (Table 1). Consequently, the gains do not isolate improved emotional editing from selection for the evaluator. Independent evaluation and baselines with equivalent selection budgets are needed.

The training objective is problematic as written. Section 3.2 defines z = E(Is), noises this source latent, and conditions denoising on the same source; the paired target image never enters the diffusion loss. This specifies source reconstruction rather than supervised editing toward the target image. The manuscript must clarify whether the implementation actually noises target latents while conditioning on source latents.

ESR requires correction or clarification. With ordinary softmax predictions, KL(eg || eoh) is infinite because the one-hot target assigns zero probability to other classes, so the stated comparison cannot yield the reported results. This could be a notation error, but the actual divergence direction or smoothing procedure must be specified.

The human evidence supports a more qualified conclusion than consistent superiority. Preference over LMS is 54% online and 49% in the small in-lab study (Figure S6), without uncertainty estimates accounting for repeated participants and images. Sample accounting also needs reconciliation: 417 participants times 100 trials equals 41,700, whereas the main text reports 417,000; the supplement reports a 27% screening pass rate and 11,400 retained trials.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. One-word prompts disadvantage instruction-following InstructPix2Pix; LMS partly addresses this, but neither a baseline trained on EmoPair nor one using equivalent iterative selection is evaluated. Affective Image Filter [30], a directly relevant cited method, is also absent from the experiments.

The architectural and reasoning claims exceed what is established. The global/local branches are not clearly distinguished from standard image-conditioned diffusion and class conditioning. Because the alignment embedding depends only on one of eight emotion labels, its cosine objective learns class-level textual prototypes, not source-specific editing instructions. The claimed human-like neuro-symbolic reasoning and enhanced creativity are not directly demonstrated.

Dataset reliability and reproducibility remain insufficiently established. Most pairs receive automatic emotion labels from a predictor reporting 73% accuracy on EmoSet, without a human audit on the synthetic editing distribution, transition statistics, or an EPAS/EPGS ablation. Human ranking of generic instructions does not validate individual image-pair labels. Essential training and sampling details, including learning rate, batch size, training duration, and guidance settings, are also missing.

Preserving scene semantics, a central task requirement, is not convincingly evaluated. Figure 6 includes replacing a grave monument with the Eiffel Tower; pixel and edge deviations cannot establish semantic preservation, and the human study evaluates only emotional preference. Within-valence editing and COCO generalization are supported by a few examples rather than systematic evaluation.
